summary: This document describes an optional extension to NFSv4 that allows file system extended attributes (xattrs) to be read and changed by clients. Xattrs let a file system store opaque metadata that it does not interpret alongside files and directories.

plainLanguage.summary: Files can carry little sticky notes with extra information. This lets you read and write those notes on a file that lives on a remote server.

questions: how to read extended attributes over nfs
how do xattrs differ from nfsv4 named attributes
subtitle: Optional NFSv4 operations for reading, writing, listing and removing the opaque key/value metadata attached to files.

tldr.problem: Most NFSv4 clients ignore application-specified extended attributes, so copying a file with xattrs over NFSv4 to another file system that supports xattrs loses data.
tldr.mechanism: A new xattr_support attribute reports whether a file system supports xattrs, and four new OPTIONAL operations (GETXATTR, SETXATTR, LISTXATTRS, REMOVEXATTR) read, set, list and delete them, with new ACCESS bits for permission checks.
tldr.outcome: Servers may support xattrs, named attributes, both or neither. Only user-managed metadata is covered, and keys and values are never interpreted by clients or servers.

today: RFC 8276 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2017. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why NFSv4 Needs Extended Attributes
sections.content:
Extended attributes (xattrs) associate opaque metadata with file system objects as key/value pairs. They are file system agnostic, and all major operating systems provide facilities to access them. Many tools preserve them together with regular attributes when objects are updated, moved or copied.

NFSv4 had no way to carry them. There is no specification of how xattrs map to any existing NFSv4 file attribute, so most NFSv4 clients ignore application-specified xattrs. The result is data loss when a file with xattrs is copied over NFSv4 from one xattr-capable file system to another.

The RFC gives uses such as tagging a downloaded file with its URL, tagging a saved email attachment with its message-id, or storing a checksum with the date of its signature. It also names applications held back by the gap: Swift-on-File, and the Baloo file indexer, which stopped supporting NFS starting with KDE Plasma 5.1 for lack of xattr support.
sections.plainLanguage: When you copy a file over the network, the little sticky notes on it get lost. This fixes that.

sections.title: Namespaces and What Is Covered
sections.content:
Operating systems may define multiple namespaces for xattrs, and may enforce different access policies depending on the namespace. Linux defines security, system, trusted and user. Implementations generally agree on the user namespace, where applications store arbitrary data and access is controlled by the normal file system attributes, so it is the interoperable one.

This RFC covers user-managed metadata only. Servers must store whatever value the client specifies and return it on demand. Keys and values MUST NOT be interpreted by NFS clients and servers, because that would lead to non-interoperable implementations. If servers ever need to act on an attribute, a new attribute with those semantics would have to be defined instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The notes belong to the programs that wrote them. The file server just keeps them safe and hands them back unchanged.

sections.title: Why Not Just Use Named Attributes
sections.content:
RFC 7530 already defines named attributes: opaque byte streams tied to a file or directory and referred to by a string name. They look similar but differ in semantics. Xattr get and set operations are typically atomic and have size limits that fit in a single COMPOUND request, bounded by the channel's negotiated maximum size. Named attributes are unbounded data streams with no atomicity requirement, opened and closed like files and cached with close-to-open semantics. Xattrs have caching needs like other file attributes.

Mapping one onto the other would be at best a compromise, so the RFC does not attempt guidance for emulating xattrs with named attributes. Xattrs and named attributes are both OPTIONAL, and a server may support either, both or neither.
sections.plainLanguage: Named attributes are like whole extra files, while xattrs are short notes. They are different enough that one cannot stand in for the other.

sections.title: The xattr_support Attribute and Basic Types
sections.content:
Each xattr is a key/value pair. xattrkey4 is a string naming the key, handled for internationalization like NFSv4 file names and named attribute names. xattrvalue4 is a variable-length opaque value. Any regular file or directory may have a set of xattrs.

The per-file-system, read-only attribute xattr_support is true if the file system supports xattrs. It is not a REQUIRED attribute, so a client should first check supported_attrs before asking for it with GETATTR, and may reasonably assume that a server lacking it provides no xattr support. Its attribute number is 82.

The protocol sets no limits on the number of keys, key length, value size or total xattr size, though the server file system MAY impose its own. A single key or value is limited by the channel's negotiated maximum request and response sizes.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can first ask the server whether it keeps sticky notes at all, before trying to use them.

sections.title: The Four Operations
sections.content:
Four new OPTIONAL operations cover what applications need. A server MUST support all four on a file system that supports xattr_support and returns TRUE for it. For file systems that do not, the operations MUST NOT be supported. Because older servers may reply with NFS4ERR_NOTSUPP, NFS4ERR_OP_ILLEGAL or an XDR decode error, clients should issue them only after confirming support.

  • GETXATTR takes a key name (gxa_name) and returns its value. The server MUST return NFS4ERR_NOXATTR if it supports xattrs but cannot obtain the data, and NFS4ERR_REP_TOO_BIG if the value would exceed the channel's maximum response size.
  • SETXATTR takes an option, key and value. SETXATTR4_CREATE fails with NFS4ERR_EXIST if the key exists, SETXATTR4_REPLACE fails with NFS4ERR_NOXATTR if it does not, and SETXATTR4_EITHER creates or replaces. It returns change_info4.
  • LISTXATTRS takes a cookie (lxa_cookie) and a byte limit (lxa_maxcount) and returns key names, a new cookie and an end-of-file flag. A cookie of 0 starts at the beginning. If one name will not fit in the limit, the server returns NFS4ERR_TOOSMALL.
  • REMOVEXATTR deletes one key and also returns change_info4. It MUST return NFS4ERR_NOXATTR if the key does not exist.

A successful SETXATTR MUST change the file's time_metadata and change attributes if the xattr is created or its value changes, though not when nothing actually changed, which avoids needless cache invalidation. A successful REMOVEXATTR MUST change them.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four things you can do with a note: read it, write it, list all the notes on a file, or remove one.

sections.title: New Errors and Access Checks
sections.content:
Two new errors are added to nfsstat4: NFS4ERR_NOXATTR (10095), meaning the xattr does not exist or the server cannot retrieve it, and NFS4ERR_XATTR2BIG (10096), meaning a SETXATTR value, or the combined size of all xattrs on the file after it, is bigger than the underlying file system supports. The RFC also gives a table of valid errors for each new operation.

The ACCESS operation gains three bits so a client can check permissions: ACCESS4_XAREAD (0x00000040) before GETXATTR, ACCESS4_XAWRITE (0x00000080) before SETXATTR or REMOVEXATTR, and ACCESS4_XALIST (0x00000100) before LISTXATTRS. As with other ACCESS results, the answer is advisory only.
sections.plainLanguage: The server has special messages for "no such note" and "that note is too big", and clients can ask in advance whether they are allowed to read, write or list notes.

sections.title: Caching, Delegations and Locking
sections.content:
Xattrs are cached much like ACLs. A client may reuse a cached value if it can be sure no other client changed it, either because it holds a delegation or because the change attribute is unchanged. Caching may be read-only or write-through. The protocol does not support write-back caching, so modifications should go to the server and be performed synchronously.

After SETXATTR or REMOVEXATTR, the returned change_info4 gives the change attribute before and after, plus an atomic flag. If a client serializes its own xattr changes and the values are atomic, matching after and before values show no other client interfered. Otherwise the client should purge its cache. When the server cannot report atomically, it must say so, and the client should not assume others have left the xattrs alone.

Xattr operations work without an OPEN, and the server does not need to check for conflicting locks; an OPEN with a deny-read share mode does not block xattr access. Permissions are still checked. Xattrs cannot be modified while another client holds a delegation, which must be recalled first (the server is likely to return NFS4ERR_DELAY meanwhile), but they can be read despite another client's write delegation because updates are write-through. In pNFS, all xattr operations go to the metadata server.
sections.plainLanguage: A client may keep a copy of a note, but it checks a change counter first to make sure nobody else edited it.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
Xattrs are application data, so the security issues are exactly the same as for file data and named attributes. Clients MUST NOT give system-interpreted meaning to xattrs. The RFC concludes that the additions do not alter the security considerations of NFSv4 in RFC 7530.

No IANA actions are required. Names are limited to the user namespace, and unlike named attributes there is no namespace identifier needing registration.
sections.plainLanguage: Since the notes are just ordinary data, they are protected the same way as the file itself.

items.label: GETXATTR
items.desc: Get the value for a key.

items.label: SETXATTR
items.desc: Create or replace a key with a value.

items.label: LISTXATTRS
items.desc: List the keys, using a cookie to continue.

items.label: ACCESS4_XAREAD
items.desc: Read an xattr value given a key.

items.label: NFS4ERR_NOXATTR
items.desc: The xattr does not exist or cannot be retrieved.

items.label: NFS4ERR_XATTR2BIG
items.desc: The value or total xattr size is too big for the file system.
